entries.name: Kidde plastic-handle and Pindicator fire extinguishers (2017 recall)
entries.summary: Kidde recalled about 37.8 million US fire extinguishers (134 plastic-handle models made 1973 to 2017, plus eight push-button Pindicator models made 1995 to 2017) because they can clog or need excessive force and may not discharge in a fire. Many sit in kitchens, garages and utility rooms of homes of every era, including 2000s-2020s houses.
entries.date_notes: Dates are manufacture dates from the CPSC notice (plastic handle: Jan 1, 1973 to Aug 15, 2017; Pindicator: Aug 11, 1995 to Sep 22, 2017). Extinguishers are purchased, not built in, so presence in a house is by owner purchase or builder supply, not by construction year. Recall announced Nov 2, 2017 (the CPSC page sits under a /Recalls/2018/ path).
entries.prevalence_basis: CPSC: about 37.8 million units in the US (plus 2.7 million Canada, 6,730 Mexico). No data on the share in homes or in homes built 2000-2025; 37.8 million units against roughly 140 million US housing units suggests many but not most homes, which is my rough inference, not a sourced figure.
entries.how_to_identify: Model number is printed on the extinguisher label; for units made 2007 and later a 10-digit date code is printed on the side of the cylinder near the bottom (digits 5-9 are day and year, DDDYY). Plastic handle, sold in red, white and silver; Pindicator is a push-button style. Check the CPSC model list.

risk.safety: May fail to discharge or discharge only with excessive force in a fire; nozzle can detach with impact force. CPSC reports about 391 failed-activation or nozzle-detachment reports, one death (2014) and about 16 injuries.
risk.financial: Replacement unit; no structural cost.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Not normally an insurance or sale issue; an inspector may note a recalled extinguisher.

fix.what: Replace under the recall; contact Kidde (800-880-6788 or the product-safety-recall page on kidde.com). Whether the replacement program is still open in 2026 was not confirmed.

entries.name: Gree-made dehumidifiers: 2013 recall (12 brands, sold 2005-2013)
entries.summary: About 2.2 million dehumidifiers (later about 2.5 million with the GE brand added) sold under Danby, De'Longhi, Fedders, Frigidaire, Kenmore, SoleusAir and others can overheat and catch fire. Many were run in basements and crawlspaces of houses built in the 2000s.
entries.date_notes: Sales dates from the CPSC notice: Jan 2005 through Aug 2013. Date-code ranges differ by model (e.g. Kenmore 2012-04 to 2012-09; many Gree and SoleusAir models listed as 'All units'). GE-brand units (350,000) were added on Jan 30, 2014. A Nov 2016 reannouncement put the total at about 2.5 million US units. Portable appliance, not built in; presence depends on owner purchase.
entries.prevalence_basis: CPSC: about 2.2 million US units in 2013, about 2.5 million after expansion (Nov 2016 notice). No data on how many remain in use or are in 2000s homes.
entries.how_to_identify: Brand name and pint capacity are printed on the front; model number and date code are on a sticker on the back, front or side. White, beige, gray or black plastic, 19-24 in tall, 13-15 in wide, 9-11 in deep. Compare to the model and date-code tables on the CPSC notice.

risk.safety: Can overheat, smoke and catch fire. The original 2013 notice cites 325 incidents including 71 fires and $2.725 million in damage; the Nov 2016 notice cites about 450 fires and $19 million in property damage.
risk.financial: Fire loss is the main cost; the unit itself is $110-$400.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Insurers can deny or contest a claim if a recalled appliance was left running; no sale impact expected.

fix.what: Unplug, stop using, and contact Gree for a full refund (remedy is refund, not a repair). Whether the refund program is still open was not confirmed.

entries.name: Kidde NightHawk hard-wired talking smoke/CO combo alarm KN-COSM-IB (made 2004-2010)
entries.summary: About 3.6 million hard-wired Kidde NightHawk combination smoke/CO alarms made June 2004 to Dec 2010 were recalled because they can stop chirping at the 7-year end of life if batteries are replaced, so owners think they work. They were sold to electricians and home centers and are common in 2004-2010 builds.
entries.date_notes: Manufacture dates June 1, 2004 to Dec 31, 2010; sold June 2004 through Dec 2010 (CPSC). Recall date Nov 10, 2016.
entries.prevalence_basis: CPSC: about 3.6 million US units (plus 1.5 million Canada). No data on how many were installed in new houses versus replacements; sold through electrical distributors and home centers.
entries.how_to_identify: White round hard-wired alarm 5-6 in across with 'Kidde' engraved on the front; model KN-COSM-IB and manufacture date on a label on the back (you must remove the alarm to read it); compartment on the back for a 9V backup battery.

risk.safety: Alarm may stop warning at end of life while appearing silent, leaving the home unprotected from fire or CO.
risk.financial: Alarm replacement.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Some home inspectors flag alarms past their 7-10 year life; no standing sale rule.

fix.what: Contact Kidde for a replacement alarm; replace any hard-wired alarm older than its stated life. Status of the 2016 offer not confirmed.

entries.name: Siemens and Murray circuit breakers, load centers and meter combos with breaking spring clip (sold June-Aug 2010)
entries.summary: About 2.2 million Siemens and Murray 15-50 amp breakers and related load centers and meter combos sold in summer 2010 have a spring clip that can break, loosening the panel connection and risking overheating and fire. Hits houses built or re-panelled around 2010.

entries.name: Central, Gem and Star O-ring fire sprinkler heads (made 1989-2001)
entries.summary: About 35 million O-ring sprinkler heads (33 million 'wet' made 1989-2000) were recalled because corrosion or water contaminants can stop them operating. They were installed in houses, apartments and other buildings. The replacement program closed Aug 31, 2007, so there is no free remedy now.
entries.date_notes: Wet O-ring heads made 1989 until 2000; dry heads from the mid-1970s to June 2001; Gem and Star O-ring heads 1995-2001. Recall July 2001; claims deadline Aug 31, 2007. Only overlaps the 2000-2025 window at its start; included for houses built about 1999-2001.
entries.prevalence_basis: CPSC: 35 million heads in a wide variety of buildings including houses. Residential sprinklers were uncommon (NIST: fewer than 5 percent of US homes have sprinklers, 2011), so the chance that a given 2000-era house has these heads is low.
entries.how_to_identify: Words 'CENTRAL' or 'STAR', letters 'CSC', a 'G' in a triangle, or a star-shaped symbol stamped on the sprinkler frame or deflector; model and date may also be stamped. Check the CPSC model list.

risk.safety: Heads may not activate in a fire.
risk.financial: Head replacement by a sprinkler contractor.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Sprinkler discounts may depend on working heads.

fix.what: Replace affected heads using a sprinkler contractor; the free replacement program ended Aug 31, 2007.

entries.name: Flammable-vapor-ignition-resistant (FVIR) gas water heaters (standard effective July 1, 2003)
entries.summary: Tank-type gas water heaters made after July 1, 2003 are built with a flame arrestor so spilled gasoline vapors do not ignite in the room. A house built 2003 or later with a standard gas tank heater likely has one; one built 2000-2002 likely does not. CPSC estimated nearly 800 residential fires a year from vapor ignition.
entries.date_notes: Voluntary ANSI Z21.10.1a standard: vapor-resistance part approved Feb 2000, lint/dust part Nov 2002, effective July 1, 2003 for heaters manufactured after that date (CPSC/GAMA release July 8, 2003). It was a voluntary standard in cooperation with CPSC, not a federal rule. Heaters made before are still in service.
entries.prevalence_basis: CPSC says all 30, 40 and 50-gallon gas storage water heaters manufactured after July 1, 2003 are 'expected to comply'. No compliance statistics found; homes built 2003-2025 with gas tank heaters are likely to have one unless a pre-2003 unit was reinstalled.
entries.how_to_identify: Look at the water heater label for 'Flammable Vapor Ignition Resistant' or FVIR and the manufacture date in the serial number; a flame-arrestor plate or screen covers the burner air intake at the bottom.

risk.safety: Pre-2003 gas heaters (in homes built before about 2003) can flash back when vapors from gasoline or solvents reach the burner.
risk.financial: None for a compliant unit.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Inspectors may flag non-FVIR heaters in garages.

fix.what: Replace a pre-2003 gas tank water heater with an FVIR unit; do not store gasoline or solvents near any gas appliance. No cost source opened.

entries.name: R-22 (HCFC-22) refrigerant central air conditioners and heat pumps (new equipment made until Jan 1, 2010)
entries.summary: Central AC and heat pumps in houses built about 2000-2009 almost certainly use R-22. EPA ended US production and import of new R-22 on Jan 1, 2020, so refrigerant for repairs now comes from reclaimed or stockpiled supply and costs more. EPA does not require owners to replace working R-22 systems.

risk.insurance_or_sale: Buyers may price in replacement.

fix.what: Replace the system with current-refrigerant equipment, or keep servicing with reclaimed R-22. No cost figure opened.

entries.name: Problem (Chinese) drywall installed 2001-2009
entries.summary: Drywall imported from China (mostly 2006-2007) emitted sulfur gases that blackened copper wiring and air-conditioning coils and corroded metal in thousands of homes, mainly in the Gulf and Southeast. CPSC and HUD guidance calls for removing the drywall and replacing electrical components and smoke/CO alarms.
entries.date_notes: CPSC/HUD March 2011 identification guidance uses installation between 2001 and 2009. Footnote: the 2009 installs used drywall imported in 2006-2007; CPSC earlier thought all installs ended in 2008. Peak years 2005-2008 are from CPSC guidance requiring fewer corroborating conditions for 2005-2009 installs; I did not open an import-by-year source.
entries.regions: Florida (59%), Louisiana (20%), Mississippi (6%), Alabama (5%), Virginia (4%) account for over 90% of 3,244 reports to April 2010
entries.prevalence_basis: CPSC: 3,244 incident reports from 37 states as of April 27, 2010. These are complaints, not a count of affected homes; total number of homes with problem drywall was not found.

risk.safety: Hydrogen sulfide odors; corrosion of wiring, alarms and AC coils; health complaints reported (headaches, respiratory irritation) though CPSC studies found corrosion not a fire/gas hazard in NIST tests of gas piping, sprinkler heads and alarms.
risk.financial: Remediation can be very large (strip-out of drywall, wiring, coils).
risk.insurance_or_sale: Hard to insure or sell; stigma and disclosure obligations.

fix.what: Remove problem drywall; replace smoke and CO alarms and electrical distribution components (receptacles, switches, breakers) per CPSC/HUD Sept 2011 guidance. No cost figure opened.

entries.name: Corrugated stainless steel tubing (CSST) gas piping without proper bonding; yellow jacket
entries.summary: Flexible stainless gas tubing is common in new homes and can be punctured by lightning energy if not bonded to the electrical grounding system. Yellow-jacketed CSST is non-conductive; black-jacketed CSST is conductive and sold as more lightning resistant. Bonding at the building entrance is the usual mitigation. This entry rests on secondary sources only.
entries.date_notes: No opened source gives the year CSST entered US housing; 1990 is from my background knowledge (flagged, unverified). Wikipedia: yellow-jacketed CSST was developed first and is the most common; black-jacketed is 'relatively new'. Bonding requirements vary by code edition, jurisdiction and manufacturer (InterNACHI forum posts, not opened as evidence).
entries.prevalence_basis: No data found on share of homes with CSST; the claim that it is common in new gas homes rests on Wikipedia (secondary).
entries.how_to_identify: Flexible, corrugated metal gas pipe with a yellow (or black) plastic jacket running to appliances, often in attics or basements. Check whether a green or bare bonding wire runs from the pipe (or its clamp) to the electrical panel ground.

risk.safety: Lightning-induced puncture can cause gas leaks and fires (alleged risk; opinions differ).
risk.financial: Electrician bonding is a modest cost; no source opened for the figure.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Some insurers and states require bonding; inspectors often refer yellow CSST to an electrician.

fix.what: Have a licensed electrician bond the CSST per manufacturer instructions and current code.

sources.supports: jacket types, risk and bonding advice
sources.quote: Yellow-jacketed CSST should be bonded (connected to the electrical service panel's ground bus) at its entrance into a building.

entries.name: Radon-resistant new construction (passive vent pipe) features
entries.summary: EPA reports more than 3 million US homes built since 1990 using radon-resistant techniques (gravel layer, plastic sheeting, sealed slab, vent pipe, junction box). A passive system can be activated with a fan if radon tests high; all homes should still be tested.
entries.date_notes: EPA gives 'since 1990' for the survey count. Model-code appendix: Appendix F of the 2015 IRC covers radon control methods; which earlier IRC edition first had it was not confirmed. Local code adoption in radon zones varies.
entries.regions: national, concentrated in EPA Zone 1 counties and states with RRNC rules
entries.prevalence_basis: EPA: more than 3 million homes since 1990 (Home Innovation Research Labs survey of builders). Divided by roughly 1.5 million new homes a year over 35 years this is a small share nationally, but is higher in high-radon areas; the share is my inference.
entries.how_to_identify: A 3- or 4-inch PVC vent pipe rising from the basement slab or crawlspace through the roof, often labeled 'Radon', sometimes with an electrical junction box in the attic or basement ceiling.

risk.safety: If not activated and tested, a passive system gives only partial protection; radon is the leading cause of lung cancer among non-smokers per EPA.
risk.financial: EPA: RRNC typically costs a builder $250-$750; retrofit mitigation costs more (not sourced).
risk.insurance_or_sale: Radon test is a common sale contingency.

fix.what: Test for radon; add a fan to the passive pipe if levels are 4 pCi/L or more.
fix.cost_source: EPA: builder cost for RRNC, not owner cost

entries.name: Arc-fault (AFCI) breaker protection in new homes: bedrooms from 2002, living areas 2008, kitchens/laundry 2014
entries.summary: AFCI breakers entered the National Electrical Code for bedroom circuits (1999 NEC, widely enforced from the 2002 NEC); the 2008 NEC extended them to most living areas; the 2014 NEC added kitchens and laundry. A house built 2002-2007 may have AFCI only in bedrooms; a house built before 2008-2014 often lacks it elsewhere.
entries.date_notes: Wikipedia says the 1999 NEC required AFCI on bedroom circuits, with 2008 and 2014 expansions. CPSC's 2004 AFCI recall says AFCIs 'are required to be installed in bedroom circuits in accordance with the 2002 National Electrical Code'. Actual requirement in a given house depends on the state or city's adopted NEC edition and its adoption date, which can lag by several years.
entries.regions: national; depends on adopted NEC edition
entries.prevalence_basis: No data on adoption rates opened; inference from code dates.
entries.how_to_identify: Panel breakers with a TEST button and 'AFCI' or 'Arc Fault' on the face. Count which circuits (bedrooms, living areas, kitchen) have one.

risk.safety: Missing AFCI means arcing faults in wiring can start a fire undetected (CPSC: ordinary breakers do not respond to early arcing).
risk.financial: AFCI breakers cost more than standard ones; retrofit cost not sourced.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Inspectors note missing AFCI in newer homes.

fix.what: Electrician can swap standard breakers for AFCI or AFCI/GFCI breakers where the panel supports it.

entries.name: 2012 IECC mandatory whole-house air leakage (blower-door) test
entries.summary: DOE's code program summarized the 2012 IECC as about 30 percent more efficient than the 2006 IECC, with a mandatory whole-house pressure test, a stricter duct leakage test and higher insulation. A house built before the state adopted the 2012 IECC (many states adopted between 2012 and 2016) was built to looser air-sealing rules.
entries.date_notes: DOE slide deck: 2012 IECC major changes include a 'mandatory whole-house pressure test'. Adoption dates vary by state and city; the numeric limit (3 ACH50 in some zones) was not verified in a primary source.

entries.how_to_identify: Energy-code certificate or blower-door test result posted near the panel (required by the IECC); airtightness from the builder file.

risk.safety: Tight homes need mechanical ventilation and combustion air (see ventilation entry).
risk.financial: Higher efficiency; older houses leak more.
risk.insurance_or_sale: HERS or blower-door results can be marketing.

fix.what: Not a defect; air sealing retrofit is optional.

entries.name: Whole-house mechanical ventilation (ASHRAE 62.2) in airtight homes
entries.summary: Airtight modern homes can trap indoor pollutants unless a mechanical ventilation system is installed. DOE's Building America says tight construction depends on whole-house and spot ventilation per ASHRAE 62.2. A house built with a tight envelope but no designed ventilation may have stale air, moisture or combustion-appliance backdrafting risk.
entries.date_notes: No opened source says when ventilation became required in model codes; the start year is a placeholder tied to 2009-2012 energy code tightening. Adoption of ASHRAE 62.2 by states is described only in an NIH article that I did not open.
entries.prevalence_basis: No data opened.
entries.how_to_identify: Bathroom/kitchen fans on timers, a dedicated exhaust fan running continuously, or an ERV/HRV unit in the basement or attic with ducts to the HVAC.

risk.safety: Poor ventilation raises indoor pollutant and moisture levels; combustion appliances may backdraft in tight homes.
risk.financial: Fan operating costs.
risk.insurance_or_sale: None.

fix.what: Check that installed ventilation fans work and run; add an ERV/HRV if absent.

sources.supports: need for ventilation in tight homes
sources.quote: Tight construction is one of the most important cornerstones of high-performance homes, but is only possible with ensured dilution of indoor contaminants.

entries.open_questions: Code adoption history; share of new homes with designed ventilation.

verification.what_is_confirmed: DOE's statement of the principle.

entries.name: Spray polyurethane foam (SPF) insulation: off-gassing and health concerns
entries.summary: SPF is used in new and retrofit homes; EPA says diisocyanates in SPF can cause asthma and respiratory problems, and vapors can persist for a period after installation. Poorly mixed or cured foam can cause odor complaints; EPA advises caution about re-occupancy.
entries.date_notes: No opened source gives the year SPF became common in homes. EPA postcard is dated April 2012. The 2000 start is a placeholder for this study period.
entries.prevalence_basis: No share data opened; SPF is a minority insulation in houses.
entries.how_to_identify: Foam sprayed on attic roof deck, rim joists, wall cavities or crawlspace; hard, tan-yellow (closed-cell) or spongy (open-cell) foam.

risk.safety: EPA: exposure to diisocyanates can cause asthma, sensitization, lung damage, irritation; vapors can be present during and after installation.
risk.financial: Remediation of off-gassing can mean removal; cost not sourced.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Odor or chemical sensitivity complaints can affect sale; roof-deck SPF can complicate roof repair and some insurer roof warranties (not sourced).

fix.what: Ventilate; consult installer; remove foam in affected areas if odor persists.

sources.quote: Exercise caution when determining a safe re-occupancy time for unprotected workers and occupants.
Skin, eye, nose, or throat irritation

entries.open_questions: Year SPF became common; frequency of odor complaints; what EPA says about homeowner remediation.

verification.what_is_confirmed: EPA health warnings and re-occupancy caution.

entries.name: Free-standing ranges without a secured anti-tip bracket
entries.summary: Free-standing and slide-in ranges can tip forward if weight is placed on an open oven door and the anti-tip bracket was not installed. CPSC staff reviewed 33 tip-over incidents 1980-2006 and 13 related fatalities 2000-2008. A 2021 GE recall covered ranges where the bracket was not secured. Bracket use depends on the installer, not the range's age.
entries.date_notes: The stability requirement already existed in UL 858 (2005 edition cited) and ANSI Z21.1 (2000 edition cited). Brackets are part of the installation, so the start year is a placeholder.
entries.prevalence_basis: CPSC staff estimate 1,700 appliance-related ED-treated injuries a year from instability and tipover; no share of ranges lacking brackets was found.
entries.how_to_identify: Pull the range forward slightly (carefully) or look in the lower drawer or behind the unit for a metal bracket screwed to the floor or wall that engages a rear leveling leg.

risk.safety: Tip-over can scald or crush; children and older adults are the main victims in CPSC incident review.
risk.financial: Bracket costs little.
risk.insurance_or_sale: Inspectors flag missing brackets.

fix.what: Install the manufacturer's anti-tip bracket; test that the range does not tip forward with a 75 lb static weight on the open door per CPSC description.

sources.quote: most manufacturers include an anti-tipping bracket
from 2000 to 2008, CPSC staff has reports of 13 fatalities associated with instability and tipover of appliances
About 132,000 (In addition, about 12,960 in Canada)

entries.open_questions: Share of installed ranges lacking brackets; recall history beyond GE and Danby.

verification.what_is_confirmed: Standards, incident counts, GE recall.

feasibility_notes: Recall data from CPSC is strong: notices give unit counts, manufacture or sale windows, and identification marks, so dates for those entries are high confidence. What is weak is prevalence per house: CPSC units are national totals, and no source gives the share of 2000-2025 homes with a given product, so most prevalence ratings are rated possible or rare from reasoning, not data. Several candidates were dropped or not made into entries because no large recall was found (heat pumps and mini-splits, microwaves/range hoods, garage door openers, ceiling fans on counts too small, GFCI expansions) or because the best sources were unreachable (SEC filings for LP and Hardie siding litigation; ICC code text; NFPA 54/70; ASHRAE). CSST is flagged: only Wikipedia was opened, no primary dates. The code-milestone entries (AFCI, IECC 2012, ventilation) give model-code years; actual requirement in a house depends on the date the state or city adopted that code edition, which was not researched. A second pass would need access to ICC and NFPA text, state adoption tables (DOE energycodes.gov), and CPSC remedy-status checks (many remedies are old and may be closed). Builder-grade end-of-life notes (not entries; from general knowledge, not verified here): 2000s asphalt shingles, first-generation gas tank water heaters (8-12 years), original R-22 AC compressors (15-20 years), vinyl-window seal failures, original dishwashers and smoke alarms (10-year limit) all reach end of life in 15-25 year old houses; another researcher covers lifespans.
